source.author: verg
source.text: Ille velut rupes, vastum quae prodit in aequor, obvia ventorum furiis expostaque ponto, vim cunctam atque minas perfert caelique marisque, ipsa immota manens, prolem Dolichaonis Hebrum sternit humi, cum quo Latagum Palmumque fugacem, sed Latagum saxo atque ingenti fragmine montis occupat os faciemque adversam, poplite Palmum succiso volvi segnem sinit, armaque Lauso donat habere umeris et vertice figere cristas.
source.text_original: Ille velut rupes, vastum quae prodit in aequor, / obvia ventorum furiis expostaque ponto, / vim cunctam atque minas perfert caelique marisque, / ipsa immota manens, prolem Dolichaonis Hebrum / sternit humi, cum quo Latagum Palmumque fugacem, / sed Latagum saxo atque ingenti fragmine montis / occupat os faciemque adversam, poplite Palmum / succiso volvi segnem sinit, armaque Lauso / donat habere umeris et vertice figere cristas.
source.text_english: He, like a cliff that projects into the vast sea, exposed to the onrushing fury of the winds and to the waves, endures all their force and threats, of sky and sea, itself remaining unmoved, laid low to the ground Hebrus, son of Dolichaon, together with Latagus and the fleeing Palmus; but Latagus he catches with a rock and a huge fragment of the mountain, striking his mouth and face head-on, while Palmus, with his knee severed, he lets lie there helplessly, and he grants Lausus to bear his arms on his shoulders and fix plumes on his helmet.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: securus in aequor haut minus Erginus, proles Neptunia, fertur, qui maris insidias, clarae qui sidera noctis norit et e clausis quem destinet Aeolus antris, non metuat cui regna ratis, cui tradere caelum assidua Tiphys vultum lassatus ab Arcto.
reuse.text_original: securus in aequor / haut minus Erginus, proles Neptunia, fertur, / qui maris insidias, clarae qui sidera noctis / norit et e clausis quem destinet Aeolus antris, / non metuat cui regna ratis, cui tradere caelum / assidua Tiphys vultum lassatus ab Arcto.
reuse.text_english: Secure, into the sea is borne Erginus, no less so, a child of Neptune, one who knows the sea’s ambushes, one who knows the stars of the clear night and whom Aeolus dispatches from his closed caves, who need not fear the ship’s dominion, to whom Tiphys, worn out by constant watch, wishes to entrust the sky, steering from the North.
